title: One act a week
hookLine: Sikhs call selfless service seva; Jews speak of chesed, Muslims of sadaqa, Christians of charity: different words, each with its own meaning

cards: In the kitchen of a gurdwara, a Sikh house of worship, the work is already under way. Someone is rolling out flatbread. Someone is washing a mountain of steel plates.

Someone is looking after the shoes by the door. Some of them might be doctors or business owners; you can't tell, and nobody asks. They're serving a free meal to whoever walks in, of any faith or none.
Ask what they're doing, and you may hear one word: seva.

teach.b: Seva means service, and for Sikhs it means selfless service: work done for others with no reward in mind.

The Sikh Gurus taught that serving others is part of remembering God, not a break from it, and the free kitchen, the langar, is one of the places it happens. Seva has neighbors, each with its own meaning.
Jews speak of chesed, loving-kindness: acts like visiting the sick or comforting mourners, done beyond what's strictly required.
Muslims speak of sadaqa, voluntary charity; hadith collected in Sahih al-Bukhari call every good deed a charity, and a kind word a charity too.

Christians speak of charity, which in the older English Bible translates the Greek word for love: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity." Four words.
They aren't one word in four languages, and it would flatten each of them to pretend so. What they share is a habit: turning your hands toward someone else, on purpose, over and over.
That's where this new week, the one that turns toward other people, lands. Not a single heroic day.

teach.h: A RHYTHM, NOT A HERO DAY.

teach.b: One act of service a week, small enough to actually keep. A week gives you time to plan it and room to fit it in, and seven days later, you do it again.

how: Sikhs do seva at the gurdwara, cooking and serving the free meal called langar, washing dishes or minding shoes, and volunteers of every faith and none keep weekly shifts at food banks and shelters.

o: selfless service done for others, with no reward in mind
a weekly fee paid to support a house of worship
a prayer of thanks said before a shared meal

games.q: which word, which tradition — tap the pairs.
p: the old English for Greek love

s: seva, chesed, sadaqa and charity all mean exactly the same thing
each has its own story and its own meaning; what they share is a habit.
the langar serves a free meal to anyone, of any faith or none
a hadith says even a kind word can be a charity
Sahih al-Bukhari records that a good word is a charity, and that every good deed is a charity.

games.q: you want service to become part of your life. what does this week suggest?
o: one big heroic day a year.
wait until you have more time.
games.why: one small act a week: small enough to keep, regular enough to become a rhythm.

practice: Let a few faces come to mind: a neighbor, a relative, a coworker, a stranger's need you've walked past.
Let one small act appear, an hour at a food bank, groceries for someone who's unwell, washing up somewhere that needs it, and pick one. Picture when it fits this week, and see your hands doing it.

wordCard.voice: Seva. Selfless service, as Sikhs use the word, done for others with no reward in mind, often in the free kitchen. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, seva: service. the word comes from Sanskrit seva, and Sikhs use it for selfless service.

carryVoice: Your line: one a week. A rhythm, not a hero day. Day one hundred thirty-eight, done.
